title: What you must reveal, and what you can still keep back
subtitle: Standard disclosure and inspection under Part 31
objectives: State the scope of standard disclosure under CPR 31.6 and the content of the duty to search under CPR 31.7
Distinguish disclosure from inspection, and explain the recognised grounds on which a party can withhold a disclosed document from inspection
Apply the disclosure statement and specific disclosure framework to a fact pattern involving an incomplete or suspicious disclosure exercise

leadingAuthorities.role: The whole framework: standard disclosure, the duty to search, inspection, and specific disclosure

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This lesson tests a distinction candidates often blur under pressure: disclosing that a document exists is not the same act as letting the other side read it. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can define standard disclosure — this lesson checks whether you can tell disclosure and inspection apart on the facts.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans on scenarios where a party has disclosed a document but is resisting inspection — expect to be tested on which stage of Part 31 the facts actually sit at.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — the CPR 31.6 definition of standard disclosure is the foundation the rest of this lesson, including the privilege material, is built on.

overview.hook: A party can comply perfectly with its disclosure obligations and still hand over nothing to read. That isn't a loophole — it's the structure of Part 31 working as designed. Disclosure tells the other side a document exists; inspection is a separate right to actually see it, and the gap between the two is where privilege, proportionality and litigation tactics all live.

parts.heading: What standard disclosure actually requires
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: CPR 31.6 defines standard disclosure by reference to categories of document, not by reference to what a party would prefer to hand over. A party giving standard disclosure must disclose the documents on which it relies, the documents which adversely affect its own case, the documents which adversely affect another party's case, and the documents which support another party's case.

Notice what that list does: it requires a party to disclose documents that damage its own position, and documents that help its opponent. Standard disclosure is not a one-sided exercise in building your own case file — it is a duty that runs against your own litigation interest as much as for it, which is precisely why the disclosure statement (covered in Part 2) carries real weight.

'Document' is defined broadly under CPR 31.4 to include anything in which information is recorded in any form — emails, text messages, and other electronic communications fall squarely within it, which is why disclosure exercises in practice are dominated by electronic document review.

components.definition: The default disclosure obligation under CPR 31.6: disclosure of documents relied on, documents adversely affecting one's own case, documents adversely affecting another party's case, and documents supporting another party's case.

interaction.prompt: Under CPR 31.6, name the four categories of document a party must disclose as part of standard disclosure.
acceptableAnswers: documents relied on, documents adversely affecting own case, documents adversely affecting another party's case, documents supporting another party's case
interaction.modelAnswer: The documents on which the party relies; documents which adversely affect its own case; documents which adversely affect another party's case; and documents which support another party's case.

parts.heading: The duty to search, and the honesty it depends on
parts.voice: structural — reference-style, building the framework the rest of the lesson assumes
body: Standard disclosure only works if parties actually go and look for the documents that fall within CPR 31.6 — that is the job of the duty to search under CPR 31.7. The search must be reasonable, and reasonableness is judged against factors including the number of documents involved, the nature and complexity of the proceedings, the ease and expense of retrieval, and the significance of any document likely to be located.

A party is not required to search for every conceivable document regardless of cost or relevance — the duty is calibrated to proportionality, which means a small claim justifies a much narrower search than a complex commercial dispute with millions of electronic documents in play.

Once the search is complete, the party must sign a disclosure statement: a document setting out the extent of the search, certifying that the duty to disclose has been understood and complied with, and confirming the list of disclosed documents is accurate to the best of the signer's knowledge. Making a false disclosure statement is a serious matter — it can amount to contempt of court, because the entire system depends on parties being honest about what they found and how hard they looked.

components.label: Duty to search: what shapes reasonableness
points: The number of documents involved, in particular electronic documents
The nature and complexity of the proceedings
The ease and expense of retrieving any particular document
The significance of any document likely to be located during the search
A disclosure statement must certify the extent of the search and the accuracy of the resulting list — a false statement can be contempt of court

interaction.prompt: Does CPR 31.7 require a party to search for and disclose every document that could conceivably be relevant, however small the litigation?
options: No — the duty to search is calibrated to proportionality, weighing factors like cost, complexity and the significance of what might be found
Yes — the duty to search is absolute and unaffected by cost or scale
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Reasonableness under CPR 31.7 is expressly proportionate — a small, simple claim does not justify the same scale of search as a complex, high-value one.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at CPR 31.7's reasonableness factors. The duty to search is not absolute; it is shaped by proportionality factors including cost, complexity and the number of documents involved.

parts.heading: Disclosure is not the same act as letting someone read it
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the distinction before resolving it
body: Here is the distinction this lesson exists to drill in: disclosure and inspection are two separate steps, governed by two separate rules, and a party can lawfully complete the first without the second following automatically.

Disclosure, under CPR 31.2, means stating that a document exists or has existed — it is an act of listing and identifying, done through the disclosure list. Inspection, under CPR 31.3, is the right of the other party to actually examine that document (or take a copy of it) once it has been disclosed.

A party is generally entitled to inspect a disclosed document, but CPR 31.3(1) recognises exceptions: inspection can be refused, or limited, where the document is no longer in the disclosing party's control, where it would be disproportionate to permit inspection given the nature of the document, or — the ground tested far more than any other — where the disclosing party has a right or duty to withhold inspection, most commonly because the document is privileged.

components.text: A party to whom a document has been disclosed has a right to inspect that document except where — (a) the document is no longer in the control of the party who disclosed it; (b) the party disclosing the document has a right or a duty to withhold inspection of it; or (c) ... it would be disproportionate to the issues in the case for the party to permit inspection of documents within that category or class.
elements: A document has already been disclosed (identified as existing)
The general rule: the receiving party may then inspect it
Exceptions: document no longer in the disclosing party's control; a recognised right or duty to withhold (e.g. privilege); or disproportionality

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact showing this scenario has reached the inspection stage, not merely the disclosure stage.
interaction.scenarioText: The defendant's disclosure list identifies an internal memo as an existing document adverse to its case. The claimant's solicitor writes asking to examine the memo and take a copy. The defendant's solicitor responds asserting legal advice privilege over the document.
tappableSpans: disclosure list identifies an internal memo
asking to examine the memo and take a copy
interaction.correctSpan: asking to examine the memo and take a copy
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Identifying the memo on the list is disclosure; asking to examine and copy it is the claimant exercising the separate right to inspection under CPR 31.3 — which the defendant is then resisting on privilege grounds.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the moment the claimant moves from knowing the document exists to trying to actually see it. That request is the inspection step, distinct from the earlier act of listing the document on disclosure.

parts.heading: Privilege: the everyday ground for withholding inspection
parts.voice: argumentative — states the justification, then its limits
body: Privilege is the most heavily tested ground for withholding inspection because it reflects a genuine and enduring policy choice: candid communication between a client and their lawyer, and candid preparation for litigation, would be chilled if every such document could be forced into the open. Two forms matter most for SQE1 purposes.

Legal advice privilege protects confidential communications between a client and their lawyer made for the dominant purpose of giving or receiving legal advice. Litigation privilege is wider in one sense and narrower in another: it protects confidential communications between a client (or lawyer) and a third party, made for the dominant purpose of litigation that is pending, reasonably contemplated or actually underway — but it only applies once that litigation threshold is met.

Privilege belongs to the client, not the lawyer, and it can be waived — deliberately, or sometimes inadvertently, by disclosing the substance of privileged material to the other side. A party asserting privilege must still disclose that the document exists; it is only inspection that privilege lets the party withhold.

components.title: Withholding inspection: is privilege available?
components.description: A quick decision path for whether a document can be withheld from inspection on privilege grounds.

nodes.label: Is the document a confidential communication between client and lawyer for the dominant purpose of legal advice?
Yes → legal advice privilege applies; inspection may be withheld
No → was it created for the dominant purpose of litigation that was pending, reasonably contemplated or underway?
Yes → litigation privilege may apply, even if a third party (e.g. an expert) created it
No → privilege unlikely to apply; the document must generally be made available for inspection unless another CPR 31.3(1) ground applies

components.textAlternative: First ask whether the document is a confidential lawyer-client communication for the dominant purpose of legal advice — if so, legal advice privilege applies. If not, ask whether it was created for the dominant purpose of litigation that was pending, reasonably contemplated, or already underway — if so, litigation privilege may apply even to third-party documents. If neither test is met, privilege is unlikely to be available and the document must generally be disclosed for inspection unless another CPR 31.3(1) ground applies.

interaction.prompt: A company commissions an internal engineering report into a factory accident purely for routine health-and-safety compliance, before any claim is threatened or contemplated. A claim is issued eighteen months later. Is the report protected by litigation privilege?
options: Yes — any report about an accident that later becomes the subject of litigation is automatically privileged

No — litigation privilege requires the document to have been created for the dominant purpose of litigation that was pending, reasonably contemplated, or underway at the time it was made; routine compliance reporting does not meet that test
interaction.explanation: The dominant purpose test is assessed at the time the document was created. A routine compliance report made before litigation was even contemplated fails that test, however relevant it later becomes once a claim is issued.

parts.heading: When disclosure looks incomplete: specific disclosure
parts.voice: direct — closes by rehearsing the practical remedy
body: Standard disclosure relies on self-assessment: each party decides, applying CPR 31.6 and 31.7, what falls within scope and searches accordingly. Inevitably, a receiving party sometimes believes the other side's disclosure is incomplete — a document plainly should exist and hasn't appeared, or the stated search looks inadequate given what is known about the case.

CPR 31.12 gives the court power to order specific disclosure: an order requiring a party to disclose specified documents or classes of document, or to carry out a search it has not carried out (or has carried out inadequately), and then disclose any further documents located. The applicant must be able to point to something more than suspicion — typically a specific document reasonably believed to exist, or a gap in the stated search that undermines confidence in the disclosure statement.

This is the practical remedy that sits behind the honesty requirement built into the disclosure statement from Part 2 of this lesson: if a party's statement doesn't add up against what is independently known about the case, specific disclosure is the tool to force the gap closed.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often think a party who suspects the other side is hiding documents should simply demand to inspect the other side's whole file, or apply to strike out the case.
components.whyItsWrong: CPR 31 gives a targeted remedy — specific disclosure under CPR 31.12 — aimed at named or identifiable documents or an inadequate search, not a general right to trawl an opponent's files. Striking out is a drastic and separate remedy reserved for far more serious procedural failures, not a first response to a disclosure dispute.

interaction.prompt: In which scenario is a specific disclosure application under CPR 31.12 most likely to succeed?
interaction.scenarioA: The claimant simply feels the defendant's disclosure list looks 'too short' compared with what the claimant expected, with no further detail.
interaction.scenarioB: The claimant can point to a specific board meeting referred to in an already-disclosed email, and no minutes of that meeting appear anywhere in the defendant's disclosure list.
interaction.explanation: B gives the court something concrete to act on — a specific, identifiable document reasonably believed to exist that is conspicuously missing. A generalised feeling that disclosure looks thin, as in A, does not meet the evidential threshold for a specific disclosure order.

testPool.prompt: Under CPR 31.6, which of the following is NOT one of the categories of document a party giving standard disclosure must disclose?
options: Documents on which the party relies
Documents which adversely affect the party's own case
Documents which support another party's case
Documents the party's own lawyer considers unhelpful to mention
testPool.explanation: Standard disclosure is defined by the four objective categories in CPR 31.6 — relied on, adverse to own case, adverse to another party's case, supportive of another party's case — not by a lawyer's subjective view of what is worth mentioning.

testPool.prompt: Which document must every party giving standard disclosure sign, certifying the extent of the search carried out and the accuracy of the resulting list?
options: A disclosure statement
A witness statement
A statement of truth on the particulars of claim
A case management information sheet
testPool.explanation: CPR 31.10 requires a disclosure statement setting out the extent of the search and certifying the party's understanding of, and compliance with, the disclosure duty.

testPool.prompt: A party has disclosed a document by listing it, but refuses to let the other side examine it, claiming privilege. Has the disclosing party breached its disclosure obligations by refusing to hand it over?
options: No — disclosure and inspection are separate steps, and CPR 31.3(1) recognises privilege as a ground to withhold inspection of a properly disclosed document
Yes — once a document is disclosed it must always be made available for inspection
Yes — asserting privilege after disclosure is itself a breach of the disclosure statement
No — but only because the claim is below the small claims limit
testPool.explanation: Disclosure (identifying the document exists) and inspection (the right to examine it) are governed by separate rules. Privilege is an express, recognised exception to the general right to inspect under CPR 31.3(1)(b).

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a recognised ground under CPR 31.3(1) for refusing or limiting inspection of a disclosed document?
options: The document is no longer in the control of the disclosing party
The disclosing party has a right or duty to withhold inspection
It would be disproportionate to permit inspection of documents within that category
The document is more than five years old
testPool.trapExplanation: The age of a document is not itself a ground to withhold inspection under CPR 31.3(1). The genuine grounds are loss of control over the document, a right or duty to withhold (such as privilege), and disproportionality.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor emails a client giving legal advice on the merits of a potential claim, before any litigation is contemplated by either side. Which type of privilege, if any, is most likely to protect this communication?
options: Litigation privilege, because it concerns a potential future claim
Legal advice privilege, because it is a confidential communication between client and lawyer for the dominant purpose of giving legal advice
No privilege applies because no litigation has yet started
Without prejudice privilege, because it discusses the merits of a dispute
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answer confuses the two privileges: litigation privilege requires litigation to be pending, reasonably contemplated or underway, which is not stated here. Legal advice privilege has no such requirement — it protects confidential lawyer-client communications for the dominant purpose of giving or receiving legal advice, litigation or not.

testPool.prompt: A company's HR director prepares a detailed internal report into a workplace incident, two days after the company received a formal letter threatening legal proceedings, explicitly for the purpose of briefing external litigation solicitors. Is the report likely protected by litigation privilege?
options: No — only documents authored by a lawyer can attract litigation privilege
Yes — provided it was made for the dominant purpose of litigation that was, by then, reasonably contemplated or pending
No — internal company documents can never attract privilege of any kind
Yes, but only if the litigation had already been formally issued in court
testPool.trapExplanation: Litigation privilege does not require the document to be authored by a lawyer, nor for proceedings to have already been issued — 'pending, reasonably contemplated or underway' is enough, and a formal letter before claim typically satisfies that threshold. The dominant purpose (briefing litigation solicitors) is what matters.

testPool.prompt: A defendant's disclosure statement says it searched only its finance director's inbox, despite the claim concerning decisions made by an entire five-person management committee whose members all corresponded by email. The claimant believes the search was inadequate. What is the claimant's most appropriate next step?
options: Apply to strike out the defence immediately
Apply for specific disclosure under CPR 31.12, seeking an order that the defendant carry out and disclose the results of an adequate search
Do nothing, since the defendant has signed a disclosure statement and that ends the matter
Apply for default judgment on the basis the defendant has failed to engage with the claim
testPool.explanation: A disclosure statement is not conclusive if it discloses, on its face, a search that appears inadequate given what is known about the case. CPR 31.12 exists precisely for this: an application for specific disclosure, including an order to carry out a further, adequate search.

testPool.prompt: A claimant is bringing a modest, low-value claim in the fast track. It has thousands of potentially relevant emails spread across several staff mailboxes going back a decade, only a small fraction of which are likely to be significant. How is the scope of its duty to search under CPR 31.7 most likely to be assessed?
options: The duty is unaffected by cost or scale; every email must be reviewed

The duty to search will be calibrated to proportionality — the number of documents, cost of retrieval, and the low significance of most of them relative to the value of the claim will narrow what a reasonable search requires
The claimant is automatically exempt from any duty to search because the claim is in the fast track
The claimant must disclose all emails without reviewing them individually
testPool.explanation: CPR 31.7 reasonableness is expressly proportionate: the scale of documents, cost of retrieval, and likely significance of what would be found all narrow the scope of a reasonable search for a modest, fast-track claim.

testPool.prompt: A party's disclosure list correctly identifies an adverse internal memo as existing, but the party then simply ignores three follow-up requests from the other side to arrange a date to examine it. What has this party failed to comply with?
options: Its disclosure obligation under CPR 31.6, because listing the document was not enough
Its obligation to permit inspection under CPR 31.3, because it has neither permitted inspection nor asserted a recognised ground to withhold it
Nothing — a party is never obliged to arrange inspection proactively
Its duty to search under CPR 31.7
testPool.explanation: Disclosure was properly completed by listing the document. The failure here is a separate one: simply ignoring inspection requests, without asserting any CPR 31.3(1) ground, breaches the obligation to permit inspection of a properly disclosed document.

testPool.prompt: Under CPR 31.3(1), once a document has been disclosed, what is the general position on the other party's right to inspect it?
options: There is a right to inspect, subject to specific listed exceptions such as privilege, loss of control, or disproportionality
There is no right to inspect unless the court orders it
Inspection is only available for documents relied on by the disclosing party
Inspection can be refused for any reason the disclosing party gives
testPool.explanation: CPR 31.3(1) establishes a general right to inspect a disclosed document, carved back only by the specific, recognised exceptions it lists — it is not a discretion the disclosing party can exercise for any reason it chooses.

testPool.prompt: Under CPR 31.7, which of the following is a factor the rules expressly identify as relevant to whether a search was reasonable?
options: The number of documents involved, including electronic documents
The nationality of the party carrying out the search
Whether the party is legally represented
The length of the litigation to date
testPool.explanation: CPR 31.7's reasonableness factors include the number of documents involved (especially electronic documents), the nature and complexity of the proceedings, the ease and expense of retrieval, and the significance of likely findings.

testPool.prompt: A party wishes to withhold inspection of a document on the ground that it is disproportionate, under CPR 31.3(1)(c), rather than on privilege grounds. What must it show?
options: That it would be disproportionate, given the nature of the case and the category of documents, to permit inspection of documents within that class
That the document is simply inconvenient to locate
That the other party has not yet paid the court fee for inspection
That the claim is in the small claims track, which automatically excludes inspection
testPool.explanation: The CPR 31.3(1)(c) ground is tied to proportionality relative to the issues in the case and the category or class of document involved — a distinct route from asserting privilege, though it is used far less often.

testPool.prompt: A claimant sends a privileged draft witness statement to the defendant's solicitor by mistake, attached to an unrelated, non-privileged email, and the mistake is immediately obvious from the content. What is the most likely legal consequence?
options: Privilege is automatically and permanently lost the instant any privileged document leaves the client's possession
The claimant may be able to argue privilege was not waived, given the mistake is obvious, and seek the court's assistance to prevent reliance on the document, though this depends on the circumstances
The document automatically becomes admissible in evidence regardless of privilege
Privilege can never be lost through inadvertent disclosure under any circumstances
testPool.explanation: Inadvertent disclosure does not automatically waive privilege, particularly where the mistake is obvious on the face of the document — courts retain a discretion to restrain use of material disclosed by an evident error, though outcomes turn on the specific circumstances.

testPool.prompt: Under CPR 31.4, how broadly is 'document' defined for the purposes of disclosure?
options: Only paper documents signed by a party
Anything in which information of any description is recorded, in any form, including electronic communications
Only documents that have already been filed with the court
Only documents created after proceedings were issued
testPool.explanation: CPR 31.4 defines 'document' broadly to capture anything recording information in any form, which is why emails, text messages and other electronic records fall squarely within the disclosure regime.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring mistake in this lesson's items is collapsing disclosure and inspection into a single event, or treating a disclosure statement as conclusive proof of a complete search. Keep them as two separate steps, each with its own rule and its own remedy when it goes wrong.
